item.title: Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January
item.description:
Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet is calling on all primary and secondary schools to ban mobile phone use starting from January.

In a new proposal from digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts, children would not be allowed to use their phones on school grounds, rules about children appearing in family vlogs would be tightened and the time children spend scrolling would be limited.

“Online, on social media or in video games, children quickly become exposed and face unacceptable risks,” Aerdts said in the proposal, called ‘Strategy Letter on Children’s Rights’.

Since 2024, there have been national agreements prohibiting the use of phones in the classroom.

The government does not have the authority to order schools to implement the policy and the education ministry will work with schools to come up with an agreement.

Aerdts is also keen to limit how children are used in online content, like family-style YouTube.

The cabinet also intends on commissioning research into sites like Netflix, YouTube, Roblox, Fortnite, ChatGPT, Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok and their impact on children.

Earlier this year, the government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media. D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15.

item.title: Nine Dutch restaurants win first Michelin stars
item.description:
Nine Dutch restaurants win first Michelin stars

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nine Dutch restaurants have won Michelin stars for the first time in the 2026 edition of the guide, and two of them went straight in with two stars.

Azurite in Delft, run by chef Mario Ridder, and Suis in Schin op Geul, near Valkenburg, both entered the guide at two-star level, broadcaster NOS reported.

Suis only opened at the end of April, after chef Ralf Berendsen left La Butte aux Bois to start his own restaurant.

The 7 new one-star restaurants are spread across the country: Nassau in Groningen, Le Epifaan in Veeningen in Drenthe, Wild Atelier at the De Echoput hotel in Hoog Soeren, Bij Sidney in Loenen aan de Vecht, De Cuijt in Mierlo near Eindhoven, Rozewied in Kortgene in Zeeland, and Ambrozijn in Valkenburg.

Le Epifaan is run by Jarno Eggen, who previously cooked at two-star De Groene Lantaarn in Staphorst before it closed. Rozewied’s chefs, Noëmie Haentjens and Ferdy van Rijswijk, also won Michelin’s Young Chef Award.

Matthijs Vrancken and Nouri Haj Romdhane of Brut172 in Reijmerstok won the sommelier award. Château Neercanne in Maastricht won the award for service.

De Librije in Zwolle remains the only three-star restaurant in the Netherlands, a rating it has held since 2004. Nelson Tanate now leads the kitchen following the death of co-owner and chef Jonnie Boer in April 2025.

No Amsterdam restaurant won a new star this year, and Daalder and De Juwelier lost theirs, AT5 reported.

In total, the Netherlands has 119 starred restaurants, the same number as last year.

item.title: Is it hard to make friends with the Dutch or is it you?
item.description:
Is it hard to make friends with the Dutch or is it you?

October 5, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Our regular columnist wants to know whether the Dutch are really so hard to make friends with – or is the problem you?

“It’s just so hard to make friends with the Dutch,” the woman seated next to me bemoans. I’m at a dinner party made up mostly, but not entirely, of internationals.

In fact, a Dutch woman seated across from us agreed. She’d recently moved to The Hague after living in Groningen for the past few years and was apparently also struggling to meet people.

It’s an oft-heard complaint in international circles.

Pretty much every organisation catering to internationals in the Netherlands has some advice for how to achieve this virtually impossible feat.

“Many locals have their own social groups that they have maintained since childhood,” the Leiden International Center patiently explains.

The city of Amsterdam sets the bar low. “A neighbour doesn’t have to become a friend (although they might!) – even just being on nodding terms with the people living around you can help you feel at home,” it advises.

There are dozens of threads on Reddit from the recently relocated who are struggling to find connections amongst the Dutch.

True to form, one Dutch poster replies: “We don’t know you, you might just be unlikable for all we know.”

While this may be harsh – sorry, direct – it’s also probably the truth.

You might not be unlikeable in an existential sense. You’re probably a nice person who has friends and loved ones that just happen to live elsewhere. But to the average Tina, Henk and Luca, you just don’t bring much to the table.

First, let’s start with the idea that Dutch people establish their social roster before evacuating the womb.

It is true, in my experience, that Dutch people maintain the friendships they made in childhood and university. This is also true of literally everyone. I concede that the country is small, which makes it easier to keep up with those friendships.

But really, most of us make our friends prior to our early 20s. You just choose to leave yours behind for clogs and tulips. Now your lineup is empty and you’re clawing for a position on a team with few openings.

Which leads me to my second point: there is a reason most of us make friends early in life. It is significantly easy to make friends prior to reaching adulthood. The foundations of primary school friendships are “The other child was randomly selected to sit next to me” and “Who wants to play the same game at recess.” You go to school all day, you see these people all the time and you haven’t yet been downtrodden by the stresses of life.

Now you need to find more of a connection than “I like playing in the sandbox with you” and you need to find the time to make that connection, somewhere between working, exercising, raising your children, spending time with your partner and remembering to order a shower curtain. (If my husband is reading this, I am sorry – I forgot again.)

Even the aforementioned Dutchie at my dinner party was struggling. It’s not simply because you’re a foreigner, it’s just hard to make friends post-graduation.

It is, however, also because you are a foreigner. Dutch people do speak English but that doesn’t mean they want to speak their second language all the time. The language barrier also makes it harder for you to mesh into a group. If you make a Dutch friend and they invite you to their birthday party, you’re now forcing everyone in the circle to switch to English.

Plus, you don’t share the same cultural references, the same jokes, the same base understanding of the world. None of this is insurmountable but it all makes it more difficult to form a bond.

If you came here looking for advice on how to make friendships with the Dutch, you’re in the wrong place. This isn’t an advice column. Making friends as an adult is challenging and you’re playing that game on hard mode by trying to do it across cultural and language differences.

In the meantime, you can try just nodding at people. Maybe eventually one of has them just moved from Groningen and is also desperately trying to convince others that they are likable.

item.title: International train connection from Groningen to Leer returns
item.description:
International train connection from Groningen to Leer returns

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

After almost 11 years, people can again travel by train from Groningen to the German city of Leer.

Services were suspended in 2015 after a cargo ship crashed into the Friesenbrücke, the rail bridge over the Ems on the German side of the border.

At Groningen central station, travelers lined up at 5:30am to catch the first train in over a decade.

The rebuilt Friesenbrücke is 335 metres long and is Europe’s largest lift-swing rail bridge. Its 145-metre central section lifts and turns to let ships pass.

The new bridge was opened in 2024, but needed additional testing before rail service could resume.

Regional Director Gerrit de Groot of Arriva, which maintains the rail service, told RTV Noord he was “delighted” with the reopening. “It is fantastic that, as a regional carrier, we are making international transport possible in this way. It is a wonderful moment,” he said.

The journey takes around 90 minutes. Arriva expects that they will see peaks of travel during the holiday season when people want to visit the Christmas markets across the border.

item.title: Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames
item.description:
Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

People with non-Dutch surnames get fined more often and more harshly by the benefits agency UWV’s fraud unit, according to an internal analysis the agency’s board has had since December, AD and current affairs programme EenVandaag reported on Monday.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief said he wants the claims thoroughly investigated and the UWV to take appropriate measures. “Your surname or background must play no role at all in whether you get a fine or how high that fine is,” he told AD.

The two outlets based their joint investigation on confidential documents and interviews with more than 10 current and former staff, including managers, at the fraud unit, which employs around 600 people.

The analysis divided 1,682 case files into Dutch and non-Dutch surnames. In the region covering Alkmaar, Amsterdam and Utrecht, 44% of the people in the files had a non-Dutch surname, but they received 74% of the fines.

In the southern district, which includes Heerlen and Eindhoven, the figures were 36% and 71%. Because their fines were also higher, that group paid 98% of the total there, although fewer files were examined in that district.

The authors recommended further research, but this was never carried out, according to EenVandaag.

Country of origin
A 2015 work instruction for detecting fake employment contracts also listed the applicant’s “country of origin” as a possible risk characteristic. When a court asked about the document, the UWV denied in an official letter that it used risk characteristics at all, AD said.

After 2020, a thin line was drawn through the criterion, but it remained legible until at least mid-2026. “I have never seen such clear evidence that it happens as in this document,” lawyer Ayhan Kara, who obtained the uncensored version, told AD. He is considering filing a criminal complaint with the public prosecution service.

The UWV says the criterion was never used, was officially removed in 2020 and has now been taken out of all documents.

Current and former staff also described racist remarks in the fraud unit. Managers born outside the Netherlands were referred to as the “Arab League”, and during a case meeting someone said the solution was “to kick all Moroccans out of the country”.

Political reaction
MPs from both coalition and opposition parties reacted angrily. Stephan Neijenhuis of the centrist D66 told AD there was possibly “institutional racism” at the agency.

Mariëtte Patijn of the opposition party Pro said the revelations reminded her of the childcare benefits scandal, in which thousands of parents were wrongly labelled fraudsters by the tax office. “It is not systems selecting wrongly by accident, it is the UWV’s own people,” she told AD.

Dogukan Ergin of the left-wing, multicultural party Denk said it fitted a pattern. “First it was the tax office, then [student finance agency] DUO, now the UWV again: if you have a migration background, you are distrusted and dealt with more harshly,” he said.

According to AD, the minister was only informed of the analysis after the paper put questions to the ministry. The UWV told broadcaster NOS it had informed the ministry in January.

Apologies issued 
Abdeluheb Choho, who became the UWV’s chairman on September 1, said in a statement that it was reprehensible that some staff still made discriminatory remarks to one another. “We apologise to everyone who feels discriminated against or has been treated in a racist way,” he said.

However, the agency said in a statement that the analysis was not scientific research, and that its data and method were not suitable for drawing conclusions about structural unequal treatment. A separate external study into equal treatment is due later this year.

The UWV has asked anyone who has experienced discrimination by or within the agency to report it to integriteit@uwv.nl.

In 2024, a reader who took part in a DutchNews survey on discrimination said UWV staff had told them to go back to their own country when they applied for unemployment benefits.

item.title: Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
item.description:
Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

US prediction platform Polymarket has gone to court in The Hague to overturn a Dutch ban on its services, arguing that it sells financial products, rather than bets.

The company confirmed the case to the Financieele Dagblad. The judges will reportedly be asked to decide whether betting on real-world events counts as gambling, which the Dutch gambling regulator Ksa says that it is.

Polymarket argues that it is more like trading in derivatives, which should be supervised by financial markets regulator AFM.

Polymarket users buy contracts that pay out in USDC, a type of cryptocurrency whose value is equal to the US dollar, if a particular event does or does not happen. The company says this is comparable to futures contracts traded on financial markets.

Fines and bans
The Ksa ordered Polymarket to stop serving Dutch users in an order dated January 20 and made public on February 17. It said the platform was offering games of chance without a licence and threatened a penalty of €420,000 a week, up to a maximum of €840,000.

Polymarket stopped Dutch users from placing bets later in February, but the regulator ruled it had acted too late and in May demanded €420,000, and rejected the company’s objection in June.

The platform drew widespread attention in the Netherlands after users staked millions of dollars on the outcome of the October 2025 general election.

Only sport
According to the Ksa, Dutch law only allows betting on sport, so a licence would not be an option for Polymarket either.

“Prediction markets are on the rise, in the Netherlands too,” Ksa director Ella Seijsener said in a statement in February. “These types of companies offer bets which are not allowed on our market under any circumstances, not even by licence holders.”

Last week, MPs voted down a motion from the far-right Forum for Democracy (FvD) asking the government to look into regulating prediction markets as a separate category within gambling law.

Gambling lawyer Micha Schimmel told the FD he gives Polymarket’s case little chance. He pointed to a 2015 ruling which found that a service can be a financial product and still count as gambling. Polymarket is also banned in France and Germany.

item.title: School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns
item.description:
School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Consumer watchdog ACM has criticised educational publishers for pricey and poor-quality textbooks, calling on the industry to change its practices.

The ACM says that for the past seven years, prices for educational materials have been rising faster than those of other products and schools say the publications are not meeting their needs.

In a statement, the watchdog said it “calls on educational publishers to stop mandatory tied selling of licences and textbooks, and to better align product supply with demand.”

One major problem the organisation highlighted is that textbooks and the licences for e-materials are bundled together, which drives up costs. The ACM wants them to be sold separately.

The organisation also calls on schools to do more research into the textbooks they purchase.

“Pressure on publishers starts with schools’ willingness to switch to other learning materials,” board member Martijn Snoep said in a statement.

Secondary schools buy around €280 million worth of learning materials every year.

item.title: Netherlands narrowly beat Serbia in Nations League
item.description:
Netherlands narrowly beat Serbia in Nations League

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands men’s football team beat Serbia 2-1 in the Nations League in Eindhoven on Sunday, marking Xavi Hernández’s second win in four games as head coach.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored the winning goal in the 71st minute in a game that also marked captain Virgil van Dijk’s 100th cap, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Teun Koopmeiners put the home side ahead in the first half with a free kick. Serbia equalised soon afterwards by a goal from 19-year-old Anderlecht striker Mihajlo Cvetkovic.

Zirkzee tapped in the winner from close range after Crysencio Summerville’s cross was laid back by Tijjani Reijnders. The Dutch finished with 10 men after Micky van de Ven went off with a hand injury, as Xavi had already used all his substitutes.

Xavi, who was appointed in August, has now won twice and drawn twice in his first four games. Germany and Greece drew 0-0 on Sunday, which leaves the Netherlands joint top of their group.

The next round of international matches is in November.

item.title: Sudanese-Dutch lawyer made minister of paramilitary group
item.description:
Sudanese-Dutch lawyer made minister of paramilitary group

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A man with dual Sudanese and Dutch nationality has been named the minister of justice for the controversial Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group attempting to seize power in Sudan.

Osama Said, a lawyer based in the Netherlands, told broadcaster NOS he wanted to bring peace to the war-torn country. He is working in politics “with one goal: to alleviate the suffering of the Sudanese,” he said.

Some 60,000 people have been killed and more than 13 million displaced since fighting broke out in 2023 between the Rapid Support Forces and the government-backed Sudanese Armed Forces, according to the United Nations.

The RSF has set up an alternative government, which is not recognised by the Netherlands and has been designated a terrorist organisation by the European Union.

According to the UN, the RSF engaged in an 18-month siege of the city of El Fasher in the western Darfur region, cutting off food and medical supplies. Civilians who fled were massacred, subjected to sexual violence and forced into servitude, Amnesty International said in a July report.

item.title: Hans Anders to stop selling camera glasses over privacy concerns
item.description:
Hans Anders to stop selling camera glasses over privacy concerns

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eyewear chain Hans Anders will stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

Victim advocacy group Offlimits says it is helping hundreds of women who have been filmed without their consent, many of whom have seen those images distributed online or through social media groups.

“Hiding a camera in an everyday object facilitates transgressive online behaviour,” the organisation’s director Robbert Hoving said in a statement. They are calling on Meta to stop selling the eyewear, and said they would take the tech giant to court if sales were not halted.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned last week that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

Last month, the consumer watchdog Consumentenbond issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a board measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Last week, Instagram removed a video by Roel Maalderink in which the satirical journalist films himself asking the employees of parent company Meta how they feel about the controversial camera glasses.
